There is even evidence that climate was a leading contributor to the dark ages and the collapse of European society--you know, the one that set Europe back by about a 1,000 years,

Even today, there are already significant changes in some areas, and one of our primary responses to combating higher temperatures and lack of water is to tap into ground water reserves. In some places, this has lowered the water table by over 300 feet and it is no longer providing the necessary resources--depleting crops, causing lack of drinking water, forcing industry to relocate--often resulting in mass migrations. It is also disrupting the natural water cycle and impacting the climate even further.

Even in the United States, the lack of snow packs, water drainage from major bodies of water, and ground water depletion is becoming a major problem. We are using far more than the natural cycle can provide, even the great lakes are being depleted at a rate of a couple feet a year. It's already becoming a huge deal in some places, and currently there are few answers to resolve them. And much of it is directly related to warming of the climate. We have depleted entire river systems because of these issues.

I think my point for talking about some of these subjects, in a limited fashion, is to highlight some of the past, and current, issues related to climate change and highlight that changes in the climate can and will greatly effect us as a species if we don't address them--it already is (although more in other places), it is just that up until now we have been able to defer some of the effects by tapping into other resources--which isn't sustainable. Climate change isn't really about if we can survive as a species, but how well we survive, and if we can continue to move forward in a meaningful fashion due to its effects.

Humans don't exist outside of the ecosystems of the Earth, we are directly plugged into and a part of those ecosystems, and what effects others, effects us.
